activities.anchor: One of the field's earliest findings
activities.caption: true or false — the independence of the axes
activities.name: gsAxesJudge

statements.s: Knowing someone is transgender tells you nothing necessary about their orientation.
statements.why: The two axes are independent — the vocabulary keeps the categories from bleeding into each other.

statements.s: A trans woman attracted to women, a cisgender man attracted to men and a lesbian share a same-sex orientation while differing completely in gender identity.
statements.why: Every combination of identity and orientation exists — conflating the axes erases the people the vocabulary was built to describe.

statements.s: The broadest definition of sexuality takes in thoughts, fantasies, desires, behaviours, roles and relationships.
statements.why: With biological, emotional, social and spiritual aspects — desire is a dimension, not a single fact.

statements.s: Knowing someone is a man largely predicts whom he is attracted to.
statements.why: Knowing someone is a man says little about whether he is attracted to men, women or both — the axes run separately.

activities.anchor: How often depends entirely on definition
activities.caption: call the broad-count figure
activities.name: gsIntersexEstimate

config.prompt: On the broadest common counts, intersex variations appear in roughly what share of births?
config.why: Between one and two in a hundred on broad counts — comparable to being a natural redhead; strict chromosomal definitions run well under one in a thousand. The analytic point is not the exact figure: biological sex is a distribution with tails, not a clean switch.

activities.anchor: If the mapping from bodies to roles were natural law
activities.caption: file each fact: shifts or cross-cultural variation
activities.name: gsGenderSort

config.prompt: Two directions of evidence — file each fact:

items.label: pink marketed for boys and blue for girls in early twentieth-century America
trousers scandalous on women a century ago, unremarkable now
teaching and clerical work, male-typed when they required literacy and authority, female-typed as wages and status fell
skirt-like robes read as men's dress across much of the Middle East, Asia and Africa
a kilt-wearing Scotsman raises no remark at home

config.why: Schools, advertising, family life — the walls need continuous upkeep, which is itself evidence of how much is social.

activities.caption: drag the divider — the claim and its limits
activities.name: gsConstructCompare

config.prompt: 'Gender is a social construct' — drag the divider to see what that does and does not say:

before.label: What it does NOT claim
before.text: That bodies and biology are imaginary, or that the field denies physiological difference.

after.label: What it DOES claim
after.text: Bodies are real, but their meanings are made: societies differ enormously on what a pregnant person may be paid, whether she may study, drive, appear unveiled, or inherit.

config.why: Those differences are the constructed part — and the part where inequality lives.

activities.caption: pair each label with its pattern
activities.name: gsOrientationMatch

config.prompt: Five patterns of attraction — pair each label with its meaning:

pairs.right: little or no sexual attraction — a distinct way of being, not a dysfunction

config.why: Researchers also distinguish attraction, behaviour and identity: surveys repeatedly find the share reporting any same-sex attraction or behaviour exceeds the share adopting an LGB identity, because identity is also a social and cultural act.

config.prompt: One line of this theory note is wrong — click it:
lines: Butler (1990): gender is performative — continuously produced by the repeated acts that seem to express it.
The way 'standing' is produced by continuously standing rather than revealed by it.
Lorber (1994): a society constantly 'does gender' — in bathrooms, sports categories, names, dress.
And then treats the resulting pattern as evidence of choice.
The empirical work favours the constructionist account wherever the two make different predictions.
config.correction: The society then treats the resulting pattern as evidence of nature.
config.why: Dress, gesture, speech — the production is continuous, and the mistake is reading the maintained pattern back as a natural fact.

activities.anchor: reads it as one fact about natural difference
activities.caption: call the headline figure, then un-bundle it
activities.name: gsPaygapEstimate

config.prompt: In the widely cited US figure, how many cents do full-time working women earn per dollar paid to men? Call the middle of the cited range.
config.why: Roughly 80–85 cents — and decomposition analysis un-bundles it: hours and interruptions (caregiving still falling disproportionately on women), occupational segregation, within-job pay differences, and explained factors — each with a different remedy: parental leave policy, pay-transparency law, promotion audit.

config.root: A colleague calls the distinctions academic hair-splitting — everyone knows what the words mean.

choices.label: Show the blob and the four problems
choices.feedback: Without separating bodies from roles from desire, the pay gap is one unanalysable blob and every remedy is a guess; with the distinctions, it is four addressable problems.

choices.label: Concede it is pedantry, but harmless
choices.feedback: It is not pedantry — it is the difference between a question that can be answered and one that cannot.

end.text: Each component has a different remedy — parental leave policy, pay-transparency law, promotion audit.

config.why: The distinctions are invisible when they are working — which is exactly why they look like hair-splitting until the moment analysis begins.
